_note: Proposed defaults for the BASP request-latency studies. PROPOSED, NOT FROZEN: finalise after the timing-only pilot and before any decision result is examined, then freeze (python -m benchmarks.run_study freeze). The held-out prompts must never inform a setting. The criteria are proposed software criteria: not achieved results, and not the hardware gate (hardware_gate.json), which is separate and unchanged.
name: basp-request-latency

regime.model: warm: models loaded before the study; one unmeasured warm-up request per arm
regime.request_context: fresh session per request; no prefix or prompt cache in any arm
regime._expert_cache: 'cleared': the expert cache is emptied before every request (both arms start equal); the OS page cache is left as it is and its state is recorded, not assumed cold
regime.termination: exactly max_new_tokens tokens; end-of-sequence is ignored in every arm; a request that returns another number of tokens is invalid
regime.request_boundary: from issuing the request to its last token: session creation, prompt processing, drafting, verification and orchestration are inside; model start-up is outside and reported separately

order.scheme: counterbalanced AB/BA within prompt and repetition; prompts in seeded random order

feasibility._purpose: is a larger experiment worth running? too small to support an acceleration claim

B.label: BASP, draft model proposing 2 tokens
B._selection: selected by the bounded tuning on the development prompts (evidence/studies/tuning-qwen3-1.7b: k=2 1.078x [0.99-1.17], adaptive 0.98x, prompt lookup 0.93x, k=4 0.86x; Qwen3-1.7B target, Qwen3-0.6B draft, PyTorch backend, this development container). Re-tune on the target machine before freezing there.

D.label: best eligible stock native configuration (its own speculative decoding, expert cache and placement tuned)

E.label: that native engine plus one BASP-derived intervention

tuning._note: bounded budget: these configurations and no others may be tried, on the development prompts only
tuning.native: at most 12 configurations per native arm (placement, expert cache, CPU share, draft settings), on the development prompts only; record every one tried

comparisons.name: internal
comparisons.permits: enabling the optimisation by default in the demonstrated regime of this runtime

comparisons.name: native-stock
comparisons.permits: nothing for BASP: it establishes what the stock engine's own features achieve

criteria._inconclusive: missing coverage, or an interval that includes no improvement, is inconclusive: preserve the result and design another study deliberately; do not add prompts until it turns favourable

A language model produces text one token at a time. To produce a token it runs every layer of the network once: each layer reads what the earlier tokens left behind in a store called the key-value cache, mixes that with the current token's state, and passes the result on. The cache grows by one entry per layer for every token, which is why a long conversation uses more memory than a short one. Because the weights of a large model do not fit in the processor's own caches, generating a token means pulling most of them through main memory once.

Explain why generating text is usually limited by memory speed rather than by arithmetic, and what that implies for hardware.

A cache keeps recently used data close to the processor so that it does not have to be fetched again from a slower place. Modern machines stack several of them: a small first-level cache that answers in about a nanosecond, larger second- and third-level caches that take several times longer, main memory at roughly a hundred nanoseconds, and storage that is thousands of times slower still. Each level holds a subset of the level below it, and a program that touches memory in a regular pattern lets the hardware guess what will be needed next and fetch it early. A program that jumps around unpredictably defeats that guessing, and then nearly every access waits for main memory.

Explain, step by step, why traversing a large linked list is usually much slower than traversing an array of the same length.

When two programs talk over a network, the bytes one of them writes are cut into segments, wrapped in packets and sent across links that may drop, duplicate, delay or reorder them. The receiving side acknowledges what arrived, the sending side resends what was not acknowledged in time, and both sides limit how much is in flight so that neither the receiver nor the routers in between are overwhelmed. The sender does not know the capacity of the path in advance, so it probes: it increases its rate while packets get through and backs off sharply when they stop getting through.

Explain what happens, step by step, when a single packet is lost in the middle of a large file transfer.

In a mixture-of-experts language model each layer contains many small feed-forward networks, called experts, and a router that chooses a few of them for every token. Only the chosen experts run, so the arithmetic per token is a fraction of what the full parameter count suggests. All the experts still have to be stored, however, and which ones are needed is not known until the router has run in that layer. On a machine whose fast memory cannot hold every expert, some of them live in slower memory and must be either executed there or moved before they can be used.

Explain the trade-off between executing an expert where it is stored and moving it to faster memory first.

Quantisation stores each weight of a neural network in fewer bits than the 32 it was trained with. Groups of weights share a scale, and each weight keeps only a small integer that is multiplied by that scale when the model runs. Four or five bits per weight are common: the file shrinks to about a sixth, and because generating a token means reading most of the weights once, the time per token shrinks with it on hardware that is limited by memory speed. The price is a small loss of accuracy that grows quickly below four bits.

Explain why going from eight bits to four bits per weight can nearly double the speed on some machines and make almost no difference on others.

For most of history a city's size was limited by how far food could travel before it spoiled and how far a person could walk to work. Canals, then railways, then refrigerated ships stretched the first limit until a city could be fed from another continent. Trams and underground railways stretched the second, and the car stretched it further in every direction at once. Each change redrew the map of where people lived, and each left behind neighbourhoods built for the limits of an earlier age.
